sentences.text: Alaskacephale gangloffi is the sole species within the dinosaur genus Alaskacephale, which belongs to the suborder Pachycephalosauria.

This animal is identified as a pachycephalosaur because of bony bumps on its skull, specifically two diverging lines of nodules running along the squamosal bone, with twelve such nodules present and the largest one situated at the base of the parietal.

Estimates suggest it measured about 1.5 meters in length and weighed 10 kilograms, making it one of the smallest known members of this group, roughly half the size of Pachycephalosaurus or three-quarters the size of Prenocephale.

Its body plan featured a short neck, tiny forelimbs ending in a five-fingered hand, long hind limbs, and a thick, rod-like tail used for balance, supported by a spine with firm connections between vertebrae reinforced by ossified tendons.
Due to the scarcity of fossil remains, this dinosaur remains little known to science.
It shared its environment with diverse creatures including the ceratopsian Pachyrhinosaurus, the ornithopod Edmontosaurus, the tyrannosaurid Nanuqsaurus, and the mammal Unnuakomys.
The only known specimen, a single squamosal bone, was unearthed in 1999 from bluffs on the Colville River in Alaska during a University of Alaska expedition in the Prince Creek Formation.
Robert Sullivan named the genus in 2006, choosing the name to reference the state of Alaska where the fossil was found.
Fossil evidence indicates it lived alongside dinosaurs like Pachyrhinosaurus, Edmontosaurus, and Nanuqsaurus, as well as the mammal Unnuakomys.

Researchers suggest that animals thriving in this extreme latitude were likely endotherms, as the absence of common ectothermic clades in the Prince Creek Formation implies a need for internal heat generation.
A 2023 study placed Alaskacephale as a sister taxon to Goyocephale, forming a clade with Homalocephale, and it belongs to the parent group Pachycephalosaurini.

Alaskacephale lived during the early Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 83 to 71 million years ago, in northern Alaska at a paleolatitude of approximately 80 to 85 degrees North.

Sullivan and colleagues argue that a specific suture found in the holotype is not homologous to that of Pachycephalosaurus and cannot be used to associate the two taxa, a view that prevents uniting Alaskacephale and Pachycephalosaurus.
